title: Deadlock, livelock and starvation
goal: By the end you can explain the four conditions for deadlock, remove one with lock ordering or timed `tryLock`, tell deadlock from livelock and starvation, and find a deadlock in a thread dump.
opening:
The transfer in synchronized and intrinsic locks used one lock for every balance in the ledger. That design is easy to trust: each transfer runs alone, and no reader ever sees money in flight. Its one cost is speed. A transfer between two coffee shops waits behind one between two airlines, though they share no account.

So the next version gives each account its own lock, and a transfer takes the two it needs. It passes every test. Then, on a busy evening, the ledger stops answering. CPU drops to zero, with no exception and no log line. The JVM could tell you exactly what happened. It just won't say a word until someone asks.

In the last lesson, four threads stalled with the lock free. This time they stall while holding locks. In this lesson, we'll freeze two transfers, ask the JVM what happened, find the four conditions every deadlock needs, and break them two ways: with one lock order, and with a lock that gives up. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `transfer(from, to)` locks `from`, then `to`. One thread runs `transfer(a, b)` while another runs `transfer(b, a)`, many times. What is the worst that can happen?
options: A few transfers run slower because of contention
Money is lost, because the two transfers race on the balances
Both threads stop for good, each holding one lock and waiting for the other
The JVM detects the problem and throws a DeadlockException
warmup.why: If each thread takes its first lock before the other takes its second, T1 holds `a` and waits for `b` while T2 holds `b` and waits for `a`. Neither can ever move. The balances stay correct, because the locks still exclude each other, but nothing progresses. Java has no DeadlockException: the threads just sit there, BLOCKED, until someone restarts the process. The first section traces it step by step.

sections.h: Asking the JVM: a deadlock in a thread dump
sections.body:
A frozen pod tempts everyone to restart it. Take a thread dump first. The restart brings the service back, and it throws away the only record of why it stopped:

```bash
jcmd                      # lists Java processes with their PIDs
jcmd <pid> Thread.print   # every thread's state and stack, plus deadlock detection
```

`jstack <pid>` prints the same dump. Each thread starts with a header line and its state. Here are our two transfers, from the demo on JDK 21, trimmed:

```text
"transfer-A-to-B" #19 ... cpu=1.79ms elapsed=34.69s ... waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
"transfer-B-to-A" #20 ... cpu=1.40ms elapsed=34.69s ... waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
```

Both threads are `BLOCKED`, and in 35 seconds each one used under 2 ms of CPU. That's a deadlock seen from outside: threads that exist, hold their locks and do nothing. Asked with `jcmd`, though, the JVM turns out to be a very precise witness. When it finds a cycle of threads waiting for each other's locks, it says so near the end of the dump:

```text
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"transfer-A-to-B":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007fb14c0019a0 (object 0x00000006f794b518, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "transfer-B-to-A"

"transfer-B-to-A":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007fb150000fe0 (object 0x00000006f794b508, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "transfer-A-to-B"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:
===================================================
"transfer-A-to-B":
	at workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo.move(DeadlockDemo.java:42)
	- waiting to lock <0x00000006f794b518> (a java.lang.Object)
	- locked <0x00000006f794b508> (a java.lang.Object)
	...
"transfer-B-to-A":
	at workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo.move(DeadlockDemo.java:42)
	- waiting to lock <0x00000006f794b508> (a java.lang.Object)
	- locked <0x00000006f794b518> (a java.lang.Object)
	...

Found 1 deadlock.
```

Read it from the bottom up. Each thread's stack shows what it holds (`- locked <...>`) and what it wants (`- waiting to lock <...>`). The header above names who holds the lock it wants. Follow the two addresses and you've drawn the cycle: `...b508` is held by the first thread and wanted by the second, and `...b518` the other way round. Both stacks point at `DeadlockDemo.java:42`, the inner `synchronized`.

The detector finds deadlocks on `ReentrantLock` too, the lock the lab uses. There the dump says `waiting for ownable synchronizer ... which is held by`, and the stacks show `parking to wait for` instead of `waiting to lock`. Those threads show `WAITING (parking)`, not `BLOCKED`, just as A thread's life warned, so don't search a dump for `BLOCKED` alone. `Thread.print -l` also lists the `java.util.concurrent` locks each thread owns.

Inside the process, the same question is one call, the one the demo made. It makes a cheap health check:

```java
long[] ids = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads();   // null if none
```

```kotlin
val ids: LongArray? = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads()   // null if none
```

Two limits to know. The detector only sees cycles of Java locks. Twenty threads that each hold a pooled database connection and wait for a second one are deadlocked too, but the dump shows only twenty threads waiting inside the pool. And JFR has no deadlock event, so thread dumps and `ThreadMXBean` are how you find them.

The dump tells us what happened: two threads, two locks, one cycle. To stop it happening, we need to know why a cycle can form at all.

aside.title: If the JVM can find the cycle, why doesn't it break it?
aside.body: Because nothing it could do would be safe. Breaking a deadlock means taking a lock away from a thread in the middle of its critical section, and that leaves half-changed data behind. It's the same reason `Thread.stop()` was removed, as A thread's life explained. A database can do it because it can roll work back: Oracle fails one of the deadlocked statements with `ORA-00060` and lets your code retry. A Java method has no rollback, and the Java Language Specification says outright that Java neither prevents deadlock nor requires the JVM to detect it. So the fix has to live in your code.

try.title: Take the dump yourself
steps: Run `./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo -Pargs=wait`. It freezes, prints its PID, and stays alive for 60 seconds.
In a second terminal, run `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` with that PID. Find `Found one Java-level deadlock` and follow each thread's `locked` and `waiting to lock` lines to a line number.
Run `jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json` and open the file. Which fields does each thread have on your JDK?

code.title: terminal 2

jcmd <pid> Thread.print
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json

sections.h: Four conditions every deadlock needs, so break one
sections.body:
Look back at the dump and you'll find four things true at once. Together they're known as the Coffman conditions, after a 1971 paper:

1. **Mutual exclusion.** A resource can be held by only one thread at a time. Each of our locks had one owner.
2. **Hold and wait.** A thread holds one resource while it waits for another, as each transfer held its first account.
3. **No preemption.** Nobody can take a resource away from the thread that holds it, so neither transfer could take the other's lock.
4. **Circular wait.** There's a cycle: T1 waits for T2, which waits for T1, just as the dump showed. Longer cycles count too.

Take away any one of the four, and a deadlock can't form. The figure draws our cycle as a **wait-for graph**: an arrow from each thread to the lock it wants, and from each lock to the thread that holds it. A deadlock is a loop in that graph, and that loop is what the JVM's detector looks for.

**A deadlock needs all four conditions. Break any one, and it can't happen.**

In practice you pick one of three moves. A **global lock order** breaks circular wait, and the next section builds it. A **timed lock** breaks no preemption: a thread that can't get its second lock in time gives back the first, and the last section takes that one. **Needing only one lock** breaks hold and wait, as the one-lock ledger we started from did. Mutual exclusion is the one you rarely remove, since it's the reason you took a lock, though immutable data or one owner per account (lesson 11 of this track) can design it away.

The four conditions apply to any resource, not only Java locks: database row locks, pooled connections, semaphore permits. Test the model on a pool of 20 database connections. Twenty request threads each hold one and ask the pool for a second. Which conditions hold, and which move would you pick? (All four hold. Taking one connection per request breaks hold and wait. A timeout on the second, after which the thread gives back its first, breaks no preemption.)

Of the three moves, a lock order costs the least, so let's start there.

compare.title: Ordered locking in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin

compare.note: Both versions take the same two locks in the same order, so both are safe for the same reason. Drop the ordering, and both deadlock the same way: Kotlin adds no protection here. One thing differs. Kotlin's `withLock { }` extension on `Lock` writes the `lock()`, the `try` and the `finally` for you, so the release can't go missing. The Java version spells out that discipline by hand, which makes every `lock()` and its matching `finally` easy to check line by line in a review. `jcmd` is the neutral referee here: both compile to the same `ReentrantLock` calls, and a deadlock in either one produces the same dump.

worked.title: Find a deadlock that hides behind a callback

steps.say: A ledger tells an audit log about every posting. A scheduler flushes the audit log every second, and the flush reads the ledger's balance. Each class looks fine on its own. Before you read on, find the cycle.

A request thread in `post` holds the Ledger lock and wants the AuditLog lock. The scheduler thread in `flush` holds the AuditLog lock and wants the Ledger lock. It's our two transfers again, with the two locks split across two classes. The dump would show it like this:
steps.code:
"http-worker-7":  waiting to lock <0x...a0> (a AuditLog), locked <0x...b8> (a Ledger)
"audit-flusher":  waiting to lock <0x...b8> (a Ledger),   locked <0x...a0> (a AuditLog)

steps.say: You could impose an order, but the cleaner fix is to stop holding one lock while calling the other class. Each method keeps its own lock only around its own state. Before reading the fix, decide: which call in each method is the alien one?

Now no thread ever holds one of the two locks while asking for the other, so hold and wait is gone and no cycle can form. The balance written with the batch may be a moment older than the last entry. For an audit log that's fine. If it weren't, you'd need one lock over both, which is the coarse-lock fix.

lab.title: Fix a transfer deadlock, then add a transfer that gives up
steps: Run the tests. Two transfer tests time out after 10 seconds: they deadlocked. The three `tryTransfer` tests fail with `UnsupportedOperationException`.
Read `Account`. You don't change it. `debit` and `credit` throw unless you hold that account's lock, so a forgotten lock fails loudly.
Part 1: fix `Transfers.transfer` so it always locks the account with the lower `id()` first. Keep the `try`/`finally` around each `unlock()`.

Part 2: write `tryTransfer`. Loop until the deadline: `tryLock` the first account for 10 ms, then the second for 10 ms. If you get both, move the money and return true. If not, release what you hold, sleep a random 1 to 10 ms, and loop. Return false when time is up.
Run the tests until all five pass, then run them twice more.
hints: A self-transfer (`from == to`) takes the same `ReentrantLock` twice. That's fine, because it's reentrant, as long as you release it twice.
In part 2, put the `from.lock().unlock()` in a `finally` that runs whether or not you got `to`. The test checks that `from` is free after a failed attempt.
`ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10)` gives a random back-off without sharing a `Random` between threads.
lab.done_when: All five tests in `TransfersTest` pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Ordered locking from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents)` using each account's `ReentrantLock`, so that two transfers in opposite directions can never deadlock. Then check your work: does every `lock()` have its `unlock()` in a `finally`?

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: A deadlock is a cycle of threads, each holding a lock the next one wants. Nothing throws: the threads sit BLOCKED, and CPU drops to zero.
Deadlock needs all four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one.
The usual fix is a global lock order by a unique, stable key, written once in a helper and used everywhere.
Timed `tryLock` with release and a random back-off means no wait lasts forever. Retrying in step gives livelock, and a lock that always lets the fast threads barge in can starve a slow one.
`jcmd <pid> Thread.print` (or `jstack`) names the threads and locks in a Java-level deadlock, on monitors and on `ReentrantLock`. Take it before you restart.
The limit: the detector sees only Java locks, so pool deadlocks show up only in the stacks, and `synchronized` can't time out. Timeouts need the explicit locks of the next lesson.
closing:
We started with a ledger that gave each account its own lock and froze on a busy evening without a word. We froze two transfers, asked the JVM what happened, found the four conditions behind it, and broke them twice: with one lock order, and with a lock that gives up.

Now search your own code for a lock taken inside another: a nested `synchronized`, or `withLock` inside `withLock`. For each pair, ask what decides the order. If the answer is "whichever argument comes first", that pair can freeze just as our transfers did.

Next, we'll look properly at the lock that gives up. What can `ReentrantLock` do that `synchronized` can't, and what does it ask of you in return?

quiz.q: Which change makes `transfer(from, to)` safe from deadlock when transfers run in both directions?
options: Mark the field that holds each balance `volatile`
Always lock the account with the lower id first, then the other
Add `Thread.sleep(1)` between the two locks
Make `transfer` a `synchronized` instance method on each account
quiz.why: One global order means no thread can hold the second lock while waiting for the first, so circular wait can't happen. `volatile` has nothing to do with locking, and a sleep only changes the odds. The tempting one is the `synchronized` method: on the source account it is still "lock `from`, then `to`", the same broken order.

quiz.q: Two threads use `tryLock` with a fixed 5 ms sleep between attempts. A thread dump shows both RUNNABLE or TIMED_WAITING, their stacks change between dumps, and no deadlock is reported. Nothing has completed in a minute. What is this?
options: A deadlock that the JVM failed to detect
Starvation of one thread
Livelock: they keep retrying in lockstep and both keep failing
A GC pause
quiz.why: The threads are active, they release and retake locks, and neither makes progress. That's livelock, and the fixed sleep keeps them in step; a random back-off breaks the symmetry. It isn't deadlock, because nobody waits forever on a held lock. It isn't starvation either, because starvation needs other threads that do make progress.

quiz.q: A service stops answering. You suspect a lock cycle. Which tool tells you for sure?
options: A JFR recording, filtered on the jdk.Deadlock event
The GC log
Restarting the pod and watching whether it happens again
`jcmd <pid> Thread.print`, which prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with the threads and locks involved
quiz.why: The thread dump's deadlock detector finds cycles on monitors and on `ReentrantLock`, and names who holds what. JFR has no deadlock event, so the first option sounds right and finds nothing. Restarting destroys the evidence. Take the dump first.

quiz.q: A report thread needs a `ReentrantLock` for 50 ms once a minute. Request threads take the same lock thousands of times a second and grab it again the moment they release it. The report sometimes waits for minutes. What is this, and what is one fix?
options: Starvation; a fair lock, `new ReentrantLock(true)`, gives the longest waiter the next turn
Deadlock; order the locks
Livelock; add random back-off
A race condition; make the field volatile
quiz.why: Everyone else makes progress and one thread never gets its turn: that's starvation. A non-fair lock lets a running thread barge back in ahead of waiters. A fair lock queues them in order, at some cost in throughput. It isn't deadlock, because the lock keeps changing hands. Making the request path hold the lock for less time also helps.

quiz.q: From wait, notify and guarded blocks: a one-slot buffer using `notify()` stalls with all four threads WAITING. Will `jcmd Thread.print` report a Java-level deadlock?
options: Yes, every stall is reported as a deadlock
No: no thread holds the monitor, they are all waiting for a notification that will never come
Yes, but only with the -l flag
No, because jcmd can't see WAITING threads
quiz.why: The deadlock detector looks for threads blocked on locks that the others hold. Threads in `wait()` hold nothing, and the monitor is free. They're stuck because a signal went to the wrong thread, not because of a lock cycle, so the dump shows four WAITING threads and no deadlock section. jcmd sees WAITING threads perfectly well; there's just no cycle to report.

flashcards.front: Deadlock condition 1: what is mutual exclusion?
flashcards.back: A resource can be held by only one thread at a time. Every lock has it.

flashcards.front: Deadlock condition 2: what is hold and wait?
flashcards.back: A thread holds one resource while waiting for another.

flashcards.front: Deadlock condition 3: what is no preemption?
flashcards.back: Nobody can take a resource away from the thread that holds it; only the holder can release it.

flashcards.front: Deadlock condition 4: what is circular wait?
flashcards.back: A cycle of threads, each waiting for a resource the next one holds: T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T1.

flashcards.front: How does a global lock order prevent deadlock?
flashcards.back: Every thread takes locks in the same order (for example lower id first), so no cycle can form. It breaks circular wait.

flashcards.front: Deadlock vs livelock vs starvation, in one line each.
flashcards.back: Deadlock: threads wait forever for each other. Livelock: threads stay busy reacting to each other and make no progress. Starvation: others progress, one thread never gets a turn.

flashcards.front: What does `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` print when it finds a lock cycle?
flashcards.back: `Found one Java-level deadlock:`, then each thread, the lock it waits for and who holds it, then their stacks, ending with `Found 1 deadlock.`

terms.plain: Threads that each wait for a resource another one holds, so none can ever proceed.
Threads that keep reacting to each other, busy but making no progress.
One thread never gets the resource it needs while others keep getting it.
A rule that every thread takes locks in the same global order.
A picture of which thread waits for which. A cycle in it is a deadlock.
A snapshot of every thread's state and stack, from `jcmd Thread.print` or `jstack`.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "We added `tryLock(5, SECONDS)` everywhere, so we can't have deadlocks any more." Explain what they got right, and what can still go wrong.
explain_back.answer: They're right that a timed `tryLock` means no thread waits forever, so the classic deadlock can't freeze the system: a thread that can't get its second lock gives up after the timeout. But giving up only helps if the code then releases what it holds and tries again later, ideally after a random back-off. If two threads retry in lockstep, they can livelock, failing over and over. A 5-second timeout also means a request can stall for 5 seconds before it even notices. Lock ordering removes the cycle altogether, so I'd use that where we can, and keep timed `tryLock` for the cases where we can't know the order up front.

deeper.body:
The JVM's detector covers two kinds of lock. `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` looks for cycles on monitors and on ownable synchronizers such as `ReentrantLock` and the write lock of `ReentrantReadWriteLock`. The older `findMonitorDeadlockedThreads()` sees monitors only. Neither sees semaphores, latches, `Object.wait()`, futures waiting on each other or pooled connections, because none of those has a single owning thread the JVM could point at.

That blind spot covers a common case: two thread pools waiting on each other. Task A runs on pool 1 and blocks on a `Future` from pool 2, while pool 2's only thread is blocked on a `Future` from pool 1. No lock is involved, so the detector stays silent. The dump still gives it away if you read the stacks: every pool thread is parked in `FutureTask.get` or `CompletableFuture.join`. *Java Concurrency in Practice* calls this thread-starvation deadlock.

For tooling, `jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json` writes the dump as JSON, and the format keeps improving. On JDK 21 each thread has only `tid`, `name` and `stack`. JDK 25 added per-thread `state`, `parkBlocker`, `blockedOn`, `waitingOn`, `owner` and the monitors each thread owns, which is enough to rebuild the wait-for graph. JDK 26 added `java.util.concurrent` lock information. JDK 27 added a `formatVersion` field. If you build tooling on these dumps, check that field and the JDK version first.

Two smaller notes. Ordering needs a unique key; with none, *Java Concurrency in Practice* breaks ties with `System.identityHashCode` and one extra global lock. And a fair `ReentrantLock` only orders the lock's own queue: its Javadoc warns that fairness of locks doesn't guarantee fairness of thread scheduling.

Databases take the opposite approach to the JVM. Oracle detects deadlocks between sessions and breaks them by failing one statement. Your code must be ready to retry that transaction, ideally after ordering its row locks so the retry doesn't deadlock again.
